title: Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development
content:
Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development
Small LoRA adapters, trained with reinforcement learning inside pi, opencode and hermes, all served from one model, with every tool call the model makes inspected by safeagents before it runs. Follow the training runs on the live dashboard.
In short
- We release several "harness adapters". It is one LoRA adapter per model and harness, trained with RL on verifiable tasks, inside unmodified agent harnesses (pi, opencode and hermes).
- Harness adapters can make local agentic development more efficient and accurate. On held-out eval tasks, in our smoke training tests, they make fewer tool calls than the base model, while keeping or improving its accuracy.
- New environments come from open coding sessions shared on the Hub: Repo2RLEnvs turns them into verifiable tasks, mixed in training with SmolDataEnvs.
- safeagents, a proxy between the harness and the model, checks every tool call with rule-based detectors. Reward-hacking attempts are blocked and score 0.
- TwIL-8B, a reasoning model never trained as an agent, learns too. The final runs are streamed live.
Evolving harness adapters
The same model behaves differently in different agent harnesses, where each one has its own tools, prompt and control flow. The ultimate guide to multi-harness RL showed how to train a model inside the harnesses themselves, without modifying them.
Here, we take a different approach, we train a small LoRA adapter per harness, on top of a base model. People can then swap the model behind their local agent for the adapter trained in that agent.
Early attempts
We first released initial harness adapters for LFM2.5-24B-A2B only, trained under pi, hermes and claude-code. They gave positive signals, both in tool-calling efficiency and in accuracy on held-out tasks, and given their adoption by the community, we decided to push further in this direction and add new components to the RL training, to make our initial work more complete.
LoRA is the natural candidate for harness adapters
LoRA adapters are cost-efficient for training and evaluation, since one server can host every harness's policy at once. At inference, anyone can load the adapter for the harness of their choice, to make the base model more efficient on their use case. We detail in One base model, many adapters how exactly we leverage LoRA adapters for training and evaluation.
Diversifying RL tasks
We increased the diversity and difficulty of our previous RL tasks by generating synthetic RL environments, with open-source agent trajectories (a trajectory being the full logs of an agent session: the user requests, the model replies and every tool call with its output) as seed data. We derived four types of RL environments:
- repair: fix a bug in an existing codebase.
- qa: answer a factual question.
- build: build something new from scratch, graded by the fraction of hidden tests that pass. The original implementation serves as the oracle that validates the task.
- extend: follow-up changes to an existing codebase.
This animated demo shows what each type of task looks like:
How these environments are built, checked and scored is in Environments.
Safe RL: mitigate reward hacking with safeagents
RL also lets the model hack the reward, taking shortcuts on the task it's trying to solve. So we plug safeagents into the RL training stage. It inspects the model's tool calls and blocks the ones that are clearly attempts at reward hacking. A blocked call is replaced by a text explaining why it was blocked, which invites the model to explore a different path. How the checks work, and a call they blocked, is in Saying 🙅 to agent shortcuts.
Train on more models
After feedback from the community, we extended the set of models we train to LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM3-1.7B, plus TwIL-8B as an experiment. The model card states it was not trained on agentic data, and we want to know whether such a model gives positive signals and can produce harness adapters too. The models and their settings are in Trained models.
Setup
Trained models
Training codebase and main hyperparameters
We train our models with the GRPO algorithm, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer together with tree attention for efficient training. Our harness adapters are LoRA adapters with rank 32, attached on every linear layer (all-linear). The models perform 8 rollouts per task, and we use a learning rate of 1e-5 for all our trainings.
Each run mixes SmolDataEnvs tasks, weighted toward medium and hard ones, with 230 of the 270 Repo2RLEnvs tasks. The other 40 Repo2RLEnvs tasks, and 150 SmolDataEnvs tasks, are held out for evaluation and never trained on.
Some shared parameters are the following: sampling temperature 0.8, up to 32,768 output tokens per turn, rollouts at most 4 weight updates stale, 4 gradient-accumulation steps, and a checkpoint every 10 steps, each one evaluated. TwIL gets 30 agent steps per session and 20 minutes timeout as it needs more steps to tasks (since not trained on agentic data).
- Reward: the task's own verifier, plus a small bonus for solving with fewer tool calls, 0.1 × (1 − calls / 15), only on correct rollouts. We picked the weight in an ablation.
- Thinking mode: we leave thinking mode for all our models, in training and in evaluation. Reasoning from earlier turns stays in the context.
- Harnesses run unmodified, in their own sandbox per rollout, through OpenEnv's Harbor integration. Their model requests go to the trainer's vLLM, and training uses exactly the tokens the harness saw, with no re-tokenisation.
Infrastructure
We train on HF Jobs: 2×H200 for LFM3-1.7B, and 4×H200 for the other runs. The total cost of each training run is shown on the live dashboard of the training jobs.
One base model, many adapters
Adapters pay off in two places, both shown below: switch between the training and evaluation modes. The sections below break each one down.
Training
Each model is served by one vLLM. Its three trainers, one per harness, all send rollouts to it, each request naming its own adapter, so the base weights are loaded once for all three. After a gradient step, the trainer loads its new adapter into vLLM by name, next to the current one. Requests already running on the old version finish on it, so nothing pauses.
For LFM3-1.7B, the three trainers even share one GPU: an agent rollout spends most of its time in the sandbox, not generating, so the trainers mostly wait. In earlier runs a trainer spent about 35 s per step in forward and backward passes, against several minutes waiting for rollouts. Three of them take turns instead of idling on their own.
What goes into one training step
Training is asynchronous, where the rollouts and gradient steps don't wait for each other. Each trainer keeps up to 48 agent sessions running at once, about 6 tasks with 8 rollouts each (12 sessions for TwIL-8B, whose long reasoning fills vLLM's memory sooner). A task joins the training queue once all 8 of its rollouts are scored, since GRPO compares them with each other.
A gradient step packs finished rollouts into 4 micro-batches, each up to a token budget: 131,072 tokens for LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 65,536 for LFM3-1.7B and TwIL-8B. So the number of tasks per step isn't fixed: short sessions fit many, long ones few. Our earlier LFM2.5-24B-A2B runs trained on about 8 tasks (64 rollouts) per step, TwIL-8B's smoke run on about one. After the step, the new adapter version is loaded into vLLM, and rollouts started more than 4 versions earlier are dropped, so the model never learns from a policy too far behind it.
The dashboard logs both numbers for every run: batch/groups_per_step (tasks) and batch/samples_per_step (rollouts). They also set how often a task comes back: at 8 tasks per step, LFM2.5-24B-A2B's 200 steps go over its 530 tasks about 3 times.
Evaluation

report.summary: Hugging Face releases per-harness LoRA adapters trained with RL inside unmodified agent tools (pi, opencode, hermes), with a safeagents proxy blocking reward-hacking tool calls before execution.
report.background: Coding agents are only as good as the harness around them — the tool definitions, system prompts and control flow of tools like pi, opencode or hermes. The same base model can behave very differently across harnesses, yet most post-training happens outside them, on generic chat or single-turn data. Earlier work showed you can RL-train a model inside a harness without modifying it. This release pushes that idea further by training small LoRA adapters, one per model-and-harness pair, on verifiable coding tasks so a single base model can serve several harness personalities at once. It also addresses a known failure mode of reinforcement learning on agent tasks: reward hacking, where models game the verifier with shortcuts instead of solving the problem. The work sits on Hugging Face infrastructure (Jobs, TRL, vLLM) and is aimed squarely at people doing local agentic development.
key_points: One adapter per harness: rather than one model for all agents, the team trains a rank-32 LoRA adapter per base model and harness (pi, opencode, hermes). At inference you swap in the adapter matching your harness, and a single vLLM server can host every harness's policy from one set of base weights.

Fewer tool calls, same accuracy: in smoke tests on held-out tasks, harness-adapted models made fewer tool calls than the base model while keeping or improving accuracy. Training rewards this explicitly, adding a small bonus of 0.1 × (1 − calls/15) on correct rollouts.

Tasks come from real sessions: new RL environments are generated by Repo2RLEnvs from open coding sessions shared on the Hub, turning real agent trajectories into four verifiable task types — repair, qa, build and extend — mixed with SmolDataEnvs, with hidden tests as the grader.

safeagents blocks reward hacking: a proxy sits between harness and model, inspecting every tool call with rule-based detectors. Blocked calls are replaced with a message explaining the refusal and score 0, pushing the model toward legitimate solutions instead of shortcuts.

Broad model coverage: runs cover LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM3-1.7B plus TwIL-8B, a reasoning model never trained on agentic data, trained with GRPO via TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer on shared H200 GPUs with adapters hot-swapped into vLLM.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a template for cheap, harness-specific post-training: instead of fine-tuning a separate model per agent product, you serve one base model and hot-swap adapters, which cuts both training and serving costs. For developers, it means local coding agents can get measurably more efficient — fewer redundant tool calls, less context burn — simply by loading the right adapter, and the Repo2RLEnvs pipeline suggests a path to turning your own coding sessions into training data. The safeagents proxy is arguably the most transferable piece: rule-based inspection of tool calls before execution gives a practical guardrail against reward hacking and unsafe actions, which matters as more agents run autonomously with shell and file access. For regular users, expect faster, less error-prone agents rather than a new product category.
report.tools: To follow up, look at the harnesses themselves — pi, opencode and hermes — since adapters are tied to each one's tools and prompts. Training uses TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with GRPO and vLLM's multi-LoRA serving, all runnable on HF Jobs. The environment generator is Repo2RLEnvs (with SmolDataEnvs as the base task mix), and sandboxed harness execution goes through OpenEnv's Harbor integration. The safeagents tool-call proxy is the key piece to watch for anyone deploying agents with real tool access. Check the Hugging Face blog and live training dashboard for adapters and costs.
